structure.title: Institutions and practices
structure.text: Volume 1 investigates American political arrangements and the habits that help them function. National and local perspectives continually interact.

structure.title: Equality's wider effects
structure.text: Volume 2 examines thought, feeling, social relations, and political dependence under democratic conditions. Equality becomes more than a voting arrangement.

people.name: Equality of conditions
people.text: Tocqueville's term for the levelling of inherited rank and fortune, which he believed was transforming every society and was most advanced in America.

people.name: Associations
people.text: The voluntary groups Americans formed for every purpose, which Tocqueville saw as a school of citizenship and a counterweight to the state.

people.name: Majority power
people.text: His warning that in a democracy the opinion of the majority can silence dissent more completely than a king ever could.

context.title: An observer's comparison
context.text: Tocqueville uses America to investigate democracy's possibilities and dangers, often with European arrangements in view. His perspective is historically situated.

context.title: Exclusions within equality
context.text: Democratic equality coexists with slavery, dispossession, and restrictions on participation. These contradictions matter to the account's reach and limits.
context.takeaway: Ask whose conditions are being compared.

notice.why: Freedom depends on repeated habits of participation.
Conformity can narrow independence without a formal prohibition.

opening: Tocqueville arrives in America to study prisons and becomes absorbed by a much larger experiment: a society in which equality is changing how people think, associate, and govern. He admires the energy, then notices the pressure to agree and the isolation that can accompany independence. Democracy may free people from inherited masters while making them unusually vulnerable to public opinion. His travels turn into an investigation of the habits and institutions that allow a population to remain free after it has become politically equal.
